\chapter{Tea, Water, Milk, and Rice}
\label{ch:bn-tea-water-milk-rice}
\hlchaptermodality{10}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can offer or ask for tea, water, milk and rice politely in Bengali, reusing the respectful verb ending Chapter 7 already taught, and say which of the four words is a Chinese loan and which shares a root with a word two lessons later.}

The chapter closes on \bn{ভাত}, whose Sanskrit root — √bhaj, 'to divide, to share' — will resurface two lessons later in a very different word. The reader offers all four drinks and rice politely in one breath (chā khān, jôl khān, dudh khān, bhāt khān), all built on the same respectful form of \bn{খাওয়া} Chapter 7 already taught rather than a new 'please' word, which is how this chapter realizes SPINE-POLITE-REQUEST-REPAIR without one. It reaches back to rescue three thin Chapter 7 grammar atoms (\bn{হওয়া}'s future, \bn{আসা}'s genderlessness, \bn{যাওয়া}'s respect ladder) and \bn{সাহায্য}'s doubled-letter sound rule, none revisited since Chapter 7-9.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chā]{\bn{চা} (chā) — \textquotedblleft{}tea,\textquotedblright{} and the first word you can politely offer}

\label{lesson:BN-C10-cha}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson you said \emph{āmār chā bhālo lāge}, \textquotedblleft{}I like tea,\textquotedblright{} without \bn{চা} ever being taught on its own. Here it is, by itself — and a new job for a form you already own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{চা}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{চা}} — \emph{chā} — \textbf{tea}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{চা}} is \textbf{\bn{চ}} (\emph{chô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}). \textbf{\bn{চ}} is a plain, unaspirated \emph{ch}, the sound at the start of English \emph{church} with no puff of breath behind it — Bengali also has a breathy partner, \textbf{\bn{ছ}}, for later.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{চা}} is not Sanskrit at all. It came into Bengali from \textbf{Persian} \emph{čā}, which took it from \textbf{Chinese} \emph{chá}. That is the overland route: China to Persia to Bengal, the same road Hindi and Punjabi travelled. The words that reached Europe — English \emph{tea}, French \emph{thé} — went the opposite way, by sea, from Hokkien Chinese \emph{tê}, carried on Dutch trading ships. One drink, two ends of the same word, arriving by two different roads.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an offer, built on a form you already have}]
Chapter 7 taught you \textbf{\bn{আপনি} \bn{খান}} (\emph{āpni khān}), the respectful form of \bn{খাওয়া}. Put a noun in front of it and the very same words become a polite offer or request:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Bengali} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\bn{আপনি} \bn{খান} & you eat / you drink (respectful) \\
\textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{খান}} & (please) have some tea \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

No new ending to learn — \bn{চা} \bn{খান} reuses exactly what Chapter 7 already gave you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}chā\textquotedblright{} — tea
  \item the offer — \textquotedblleft{}chā khān\textquotedblright{}
  \item the route it travelled — \textquotedblleft{}chá … čā … chā\textquotedblright{}
  \item last lesson's line again — \textquotedblleft{}āmār chā bhālo lāge\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Offer someone tea, politely. (\textbf{\bn{চা} \bn{খান}.}) Is \bn{চা} inherited from Sanskrit? (\textbf{No} — it is a Chinese word that reached Bengali by way of Persian.) What form does \bn{চা} \bn{খান} reuse? (\textbf{\bn{আপনি} \bn{খান}}, Chapter 7's respectful \textquotedblleft{}you eat/drink,\textquotedblright{} with no new ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jôl]{\bn{জল} (jôl) — \textquotedblleft{}water,\textquotedblright{} prised out of a phrase you already know}

\label{lesson:BN-C10-jol}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 7 taught you \textbf{\bn{জল} \bn{খাওয়া}}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink water\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}water-eat\textquotedblright{} — without ever teaching \bn{জল} by itself. Here it is, on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{জল}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{জল}} — \emph{jôl} — \textbf{water}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{জল} \bn{খান}} — (please) drink some water, the same offer pattern as last lesson.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{জল}} is \textbf{\bn{জ}} (\emph{jô}) + \textbf{\bn{ল}} (\emph{l}), two bare consonants with no vowel sign between them. \textbf{\bn{জ}} keeps its inherent vowel; \textbf{\bn{ল}}, at the end of the word with nothing written after it, is silent — so \emph{jôl}, one syllable, not \emph{jô-lô}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{জল}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{জল}} (\emph{jala}), inherited straight through Prakrit. Past Sanskrit its root is genuinely unsettled: one proposal traces it to PIE \textbf{*g\textsuperscript{w}elHo-}, \textquotedblleft{}to gush forth, to spring\textquotedblright{} — but the same sources call a local, non-Indo-European origin \textquotedblleft{}unlikely though possible.\textquotedblright{} No confident cousin is claimed here; the honest answer is that nobody is sure.

Bengali has a second word for water, most common in Bangladesh: \textbf{\bn{পানি}} (\emph{pani}). That one \emph{is} on secure ground — Sanskrit \textbf{pānīya}, \textquotedblleft{}drinkable,\textquotedblright{} built directly on \textbf{√pā}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink,\textquotedblright{} the very root behind Chapter 7's \textbf{\bn{পান} \bn{করা}} and English \textbf{potion}, \textbf{potable}. Two words for the same thing, one of disputed origin and one you can trace all the way home.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}jôl\textquotedblright{} — water, one syllable
  \item the offer — \textquotedblleft{}jôl khān\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Bangladesh word, and its root — \textquotedblleft{}pani … pā, potion, potable\textquotedblright{}
  \item tea, then water — \textquotedblleft{}chā khān … jôl khān\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Chapter 7 already say with \bn{জল}, without teaching it as a word? (\textbf{\bn{জল} \bn{খাওয়া}}, \textquotedblleft{}to drink water.\textquotedblright{}) Is \bn{জল}'s root secure? (\textbf{No} — genuinely disputed.) Which everyday synonym for water traces cleanly to \textquotedblleft{}drinkable,\textquotedblright{} from the root behind \emph{potion}? (\textbf{\bn{পানি}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dudh]{\bn{দুধ} (dudh) — \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} and the vowel this word refuses to keep}

\label{lesson:BN-C10-dudh}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 9 met a word that had to end in a vowel nobody wrote — \bn{সাহায্য}, \emph{sāhājjo}. This word looks like it could do the same thing. It doesn't.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{দুধ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{দুধ}} — \emph{dudh} — \textbf{milk}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{দুধ} \bn{খান}} — (please) have some milk.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{দুধ}} is \textbf{\bn{দ}} (\emph{dô}) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{ু}} (\emph{u}), plus \textbf{\bn{ধ}} (\emph{dh}), a breathy dental \emph{d}. Nothing is written after \bn{ধ} — the same bare-consonant ending \bn{সাহায্য} had.

\begin{sounds}
\bn{সাহায্য} had to surface its inherent vowel — \emph{sāhājj\textbf{o}}, not \emph{sāhājj} — because its final letter is a doubled consonant, \textbf{\bn{য্য}}, and a bare cluster like that cannot be said at all without a vowel to carry it. \bn{দুধ} ends in one plain consonant, \bn{ধ}, which needs no such help. So Bengali leaves it silent: \textbf{\bn{দুধ}}, not \emph{dudho}. The spelling looks the same kind of \textquotedblleft{}bare ending\textquotedblright{} in both words; whether the vowel survives depends on what it would take to pronounce the letter beneath it.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{দুধ}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{দুগ্ধ}} (\emph{dugdha}), the past participle of \textbf{√\bn{দুহ্}} (\emph{√duh}, \textquotedblleft{}to milk\textquotedblright{}), from PIE \textbf{*d\textsuperscript{h}ewg\textsuperscript{h}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to produce, to yield.\textquotedblright{} That root has exactly one secure English descendant, and it is not the word you would guess: \textbf{doughty}, \textquotedblleft{}valiant,\textquotedblright{} through Old English \emph{dohtig}, \textquotedblleft{}capable, of use.\textquotedblright{} The word that \emph{looks} like a cousin, \textbf{dough}, is not one — it comes from a completely different PIE root, \textbf{*d\textsuperscript{h}eyǵ\textsuperscript{h}-}, \textquotedblleft{}to knead, to mould.\textquotedblright{} A close sound, two unrelated histories.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dudh\textquotedblright{} — no trailing vowel
  \item the offer — \textquotedblleft{}dudh khān\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two endings compared — \textquotedblleft{}sāhājjo … dudh\textquotedblright{}
  \item three drinks so far — \textquotedblleft{}chā khān … jôl khān … dudh khān\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \bn{সাহায্য} keep its final vowel while \bn{দুধ} doesn't? (\textbf{\bn{সাহায্য} ends in a doubled consonant that cannot be said bare; \bn{দুধ}'s single \bn{ধ} can.}) Is \bn{দুধ}'s root related to English \emph{dough}? (\textbf{No} — that is a different PIE root; the real cousin is \emph{doughty}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhāt]{\bn{ভাত} (bhāt) — \textquotedblleft{}rice,\textquotedblright{} and a root that will name a person too}

\label{lesson:BN-C10-bhat}



\begin{quote}
Three drinks so far. This chapter closes on the word for the meal itself — and a root worth remembering, because it comes back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \bn{ভাত}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\bn{ভাত}} — \emph{bhāt} — \textbf{cooked rice}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\bn{ভাত} \bn{খান}} — (please) eat some rice; in everyday Bengali, \textquotedblleft{}have a meal.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\bn{ভাত}} is \textbf{\bn{ভ}} (\emph{bhô}, a \emph{b} with a puff of breath) with the vowel sign \textbf{\bn{া}} (\emph{ā}), plus \textbf{\bn{ত}} (\emph{t}), silent at the end for the same reason \bn{দুধ}'s \bn{ধ} was: a single bare consonant needs no vowel to carry it, so \emph{bhāt}, not \emph{bhāto}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\bn{ভাত}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\bn{ভক্ত}} (\emph{bhakta}), \textquotedblleft{}portioned out, shared\textquotedblright{} — the past participle of \textbf{√\bn{ভজ্}} (\emph{√bhaj}), \textquotedblleft{}to divide, to distribute, to allot.\textquotedblright{} PIE \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}eh\textsubscript{2}g-} sits behind it. Rice, in this word's own history, is not \textquotedblleft{}the grain\textquotedblright{} but \textbf{the share that was given out} — the meal as a portion handed to you.

Hold onto that root. Two lessons from now, the very same Sanskrit verb will turn up again, naming someone rather than something.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhāt\textquotedblright{} — cooked rice, no trailing vowel
  \item the offer — \textquotedblleft{}bhāt khān\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four, in order — \textquotedblleft{}chā khān … jôl khān … dudh khān … bhāt khān\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two silent endings, back to back — \textquotedblleft{}dudh … bhāt\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root that shares — \textquotedblleft{}bhaj — to divide, to distribute\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \bn{ভাত} literally mean, at the root? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Portioned out, shared\textquotedblright{} — √bhaj, \textquotedblleft{}to divide.\textquotedblright{}}) Offer all four of this chapter's words, politely, in one breath. (\textbf{Chā khān, jôl khān, dudh khān, bhāt khān.}) Why do \bn{দুধ} and \bn{ভাত} both drop their final vowel? (\textbf{Each ends in one plain consonant, easily said bare.}) A quick run back through Chapter 7 while you're at it: which verb does Bengali reach for when \bn{আছে} runs out of future? (\textbf{\bn{হবে}.}) How many forms of \textquotedblleft{}I come\textquotedblright{} does a Bengali speaker need, whoever is talking? (\textbf{One} — \emph{āmi āsi}.) And \textquotedblleft{}you go\textquotedblright{} to a stranger, versus to a friend? (\textbf{\bn{যান}} \emph{jān}, versus \textbf{\bn{যাও}} \emph{jāo}.) \bn{সাহায্য}'s doubled letter — said how? (\textbf{jj}, not \emph{yy}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
